snippet.textDisplay:
​@jimkuan8493 My friend, you need to relearn history.
Lunar New Year is not of Chinese origin. It is a very ancient agricultural festival linked to the wet rice cycle, the spring renewal, and offerings to ancestors/earth-sky, which already existed among the Bách Việt people (including the Lạc Việt, ancestors of the Vietnamese) long before Han domination (111 BCE).

The main evidence is that the date of the New Year changed considerably under the different Chinese dynasties, showing that it was not a fixed "original Chinese" tradition, but a calendar system adapted over time, influenced by older practices from the South (Bách Việt regions).

Under the Xia dynasty (legendary, ~2070-1600 BCE): the first month was often in the spring. Under the Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BCE): the 12th lunar month was used as the beginning of the year.

Under the Zhou dynasty (c. 1046-256 BCE): the 11th month (around the winter solstice) was reinstated.

Under the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE): Qin Shi Huang moved the New Year to the 10th lunar month to mark his rise to power.

Under the Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE): the "modern" date was fixed on the first day of the first lunar month (after the winter solstice), a date that has remained largely unchanged to this day.

These multiple changes show that the "Lunar New Year" was not a purely northern Chinese invention, but a shared and adapted heritage of older Southeast Asian agricultural traditions (including Bách Việt). This includes bánh chưng/bánh giầy (a legend of the Hùng Vương, predating the Han dynasty), and especially its direct link to the rice-growing cycle of the Red River Delta.

In short: the festival itself (end of harvest, renewal, family, offerings) is an indigenous Bách Việt tradition, much older than Chinese dynastic adjustments. Tết is Vietnamese at heart, not "copied Chinese"!

These multiple changes show that the "Lunar New Year" was not a purely northern Chinese invention, but a shared and adapted heritage of older Southeast Asian agricultural traditions (including Bách Việt). This includes bánh chưng/bánh giầy (a legend of the Hùng Vương, predating the Han dynasty), and especially its direct link to the rice-growing cycle of the Red River Delta.

In short: the festival itself (end of harvest, renewal, family, offerings) is an indigenous Bách Việt tradition, much older than Chinese dynastic adjustments. Tết is Vietnamese at heart, not "copied Chinese"!

snippet.textDisplay:
China has officially begun deploying humanoid robots for patrol and logistics duties along its border with 

Vietnam

. This initiative, part of a broader push to integrate "embodied AI" into public security, primarily utilizes the Walker S2 model developed by UBTECH Robotics. 

Key Deployment Details

Location: The primary rollout is centered in the Guangxi region, specifically at border crossings in the coastal city of Fangchenggang.

The Contract: UBTECH secured a 264 million yuan (US$37 million) deal to supply these industrial-grade humanoids.

Primary Tasks: Unlike science-fiction "soldier" tropes, these robots are currently tasked with:

Guiding travelers and managing crowd flow at checkpoints.

Assisting in security patrols and cargo inspections.

Handling logistics and monitoring safety hazards at nearby industrial sites (e.g., steel and aluminum plants).

The humanoid robots featured in China's Spring Festival Gala may appear intelligent, but in reality, they are merely "machines" proficient in specific skills; they don't even possess intelligence grounded in "common sense."
Google previously spent hundreds of billions of dollars developing "autonomous driving," yet why did they ultimately decide to abandon it?
Google also spent a fortune acquiring Boston Dynamics, only to eventually sell it to Japan's SoftBank. Why?
Google's engineers and scientists are among the smartest people in the world; why would they make such moves?
Because Google is no longer willing to waste vast sums of money on "hollow" AI just for show.
Google has woken up, while China is still asleep—still burning through money just to put on a theatrical AI performance. Do you get it?
China really needs to reflect deeply: What is the true meaning behind exhausting the entire nation's resources and wealth to develop "machines" that merely possess technical proficiency but lack common sense?

snippet.textDisplay:
网上大多数人都是无知混混。让我给你们说说机器人的内幕。
比较一下美国机器人和中国机器人。 我说些别人没有想到的东西。
20多年前我来美国，就在shopping mall里看到机器人和人对话，那个机器人所有的动作就是转头和举手臂。但它能和人对答如流。后来我醒悟到，那个机器人的背后其实有个人。他不一定在现场，但可以通过麦克风和人对话，外加些变声。我为何要说这个呢？ 因为中国机器人表演后面还有人拿遥控器操作。 这本质上和20年前的是一回事。好吧，我承认这次的机器人表现不全是遥控器。 

那么美国机器人和中国机器人有什么区别呢？ 众所周知，中国机器人的飞速发展是近几年的事，你们知道为何？ 因为波士顿动力开源机器人代码。 我十分肯定，中国机器人的动作是按事先编好的程序在表演，而不是随机按场景做动作。 而美国机器人是后者。美国机器人是为特定工作目的设计的。他们的目的是干活。而中国机器人的目的是表演。美国可以把翻跟头做的更加好，只是人家没那个必要。这就像MMA和中国功夫。目的不同。

说半天不能不表扬一下中国机器人。我认为中国机器人在保持平衡方面有很大进步。这是向前迈出的一大步。也是机器人发展的第一步。不能保持平衡，下面什么都没法做。比较美中机器人，美国的要壮实很多，我估计重量也比中国高很多，原因是人家的机器人是为干活设计的。而中国机器人的目的是表演，所以做的比较小和轻，容易翻跟头。如果中国机器人做成美国那么笨重，翻跟头就没那么容易了。

保持平衡是机器人的第一步。人家波士顿动力10年前就做到了。10年前波士顿动力机器人就可以前后空翻。 人家机器人还可以搬很重的铁块，翻桌子，走独木桥，跨围栏，前后左右行走。。。。就单从保持平衡上说，其难度在翻跟头之上。保持平衡中隐藏一个算法，怎么让身体协调，使得自己不摔倒。 波士顿动力开源这个算法的代码。这是导致中国机器人会跳舞的关键。关节节点数量是衡量机器人水平的重要因数。 很明显，波士顿动力比中国多很多。这表明人家控制机器人的复杂程度远高于中国。更不要说人家机器人可以按场景自己控制行为。中国机器人完全就是按编好的指令跳舞。除了跳舞还会什么？ 根本不是一个等级的东西。中国机器人像蚂蚱似的蹦跶，人家机器人像小号擎天柱,可以干活，更加接近真人。

至于最后谁能干过谁。这个就很难说了。毕竟以一个公司的力量去对抗另外一个国家，如果美国政府或大财团不出手的话，是很困难的事。保护自己的唯一办法，就是不要让别人知道你在干什么。这是美国公司的短处。
 那么中国公司的短处在哪里？ 继续等待人家开源。

According to public reports, China has made several key statements within the framework of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) on the military application of artificial intelligence:
In 2018, China submitted its first position paper, calling on the international community to focus on the risks posed by lethal autonomous weapon systems.
In 2021, China proposed that AI weapons must remain under human control and opposed the use of AI in the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
In 2023, China explicitly opposed allowing weapons systems full autonomy in lethal decision‑making, and insisted on a “human-in-the-loop” and human-machine integrated control model.
China has also reiterated these positions at forums such as the World Artificial Intelligence Conference.
Countries including the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, and Israel have expressed opposition or reservations about these proposals.
China’s development of AI and robotics is a strategic choice to actively promote industrial upgrading and achieve self-reliance in science and technology. At the same time, it is committed to the responsible governance of military AI to uphold international humanitarian and security principles.

snippet.textDisplay:
The Robots Danced: A Thesis on China's AI Trajectory

On the evening of the 2026 Spring Festival Gala, 1.4 billion viewers witnessed something extraordinary. Robots moved alongside children in seamless choreography—not as mechanical marvels drawing attention to their own complexity, but as natural participants in artistic expression. They did not perform tricks that interrupted flow. They danced. When explosive power was needed, their legs delivered. But the seamlessness—the quality that made the performance breathtaking—came from something deeper: what a human would call core stabilizers. These robots moved as if designed with muscles no one sees, enabling transitions so fluid that technology itself became invisible.

This moment was not merely entertainment. It was a civilizational statement about what kind of AI future China is building.

The prevailing Western narrative of the AI race, fixated on semiconductor supremacy measured in nanometers and raw compute, fundamentally misjudges the nature of this technological revolution. Strategic advantage in the AI epoch will be determined not by who designs the most powerful chips, but by which society achieves the most pervasive, sophisticated integration of AI into its economic fabric and daily life. By this metric—the application imperative—China is not lagging but establishing a formidable, self-reinforcing lead.

Evidence spans multiple domains. While Tesla tests robotaxis in limited fleets, fully commercialized autonomous vehicles already serve the public at scale across Chinese cities. In drones, Chinese firms dominate global markets. In manufacturing, AI is the linchpin of the world's largest automated production base. The Gala performance simply made visible what has been unfolding across Chinese society: the normalization of intelligent systems to the point of cultural absorption.

This application leadership is structural. China's vast, digitally-adept population provides an unparalleled testbed for rapid iteration. snippet.textDisplay:
It isn’t simply about hostility toward China. At its core, it’s about anxiety over losing control of the global narrative. The modern world has been shaped largely by Western cultural norms, institutions, and values. When influence shifts from one Western power to another, the transition tends to meet less resistance because the overarching narrative remains within the same cultural framework.

China’s rise represents something fundamentally different. For the first time in modern history, the authority to shape the global narrative is being seriously contested by a non-Western power. And whoever shapes the narrative holds immense influence—over what is considered legitimate or illegitimate, acceptable or unacceptable, even true or false.

The struggle, then, is not merely geopolitical. It is about who defines the story the world tells about itself.

snippet.textDisplay:
That statement mixes accurate historical facts with selective framing to create a narrative of continuous Chinese technological primacy, which does not reflect the full historical progression.

Yes, China as a civilization produced major early inventions—paper, the compass, printing, and gunpowder. Those were important enabling tools. But those inventions alone did not create modern technological civilization. The decisive transition came later, when Europe developed the scientific method, Enlightenment rationalism, and institutionalized continuous innovation. That produced modern physics, industrialization, electricity, computing, aviation, and the internet—the actual technological architecture of the modern world.

China’s modern technological rise did not occur in isolation. It accelerated after economic liberalization beginning in 1978 and integration into global trade, particularly with Western markets. This provided access to capital, engineering ecosystems, and global supply chains. China’s strength today is most evident in engineering scale, manufacturing integration, and infrastructure deployment.

It is also important to distinguish between cost efficiency and foundational innovation. Low labor costs, centralized industrial policy, and supply chain concentration contributed significantly to China’s manufacturing expansion. Over time, China has developed genuine engineering capability, but most foundational modern technologies—transistors, microprocessors, operating systems, jet engines, and the internet—originated elsewhere.

Because we live in the internet era, this progression is publicly verifiable. The scientific papers, patent records, engineering lineages, and technological dependencies are all documented. China is now a major technological power and competitor, but its rise occurred through integration into a technological system whose foundational architecture was established earlier through scientific and industrial developments outside China.

China’s early inventions were historically important. Its modern rise is real. But the continuity implied by that statement—from ancient invention directly to modern technological leadership—omits the critical intervening development of modern scientific and industrial systems.

This provided access to capital, engineering ecosystems, and global supply chains. China’s strength today is most evident in engineering scale, manufacturing integration, and infrastructure deployment.

It is also important to distinguish between cost efficiency and foundational innovation. Low labor costs, centralized industrial policy, and supply chain concentration contributed significantly to China’s manufacturing expansion. Over time, China has developed genuine engineering capability, but most foundational modern technologies—transistors, microprocessors, operating systems, jet engines, and the internet—originated elsewhere.

@joannelim5483 1: The Argument’s Structure
The argument follows this implicit chain:
Premise 1: China invented paper, compass, printing, gunpowder. (True)
Premise 2: These inventions were foundational to the modern era. (Partially true, but incomplete)
Premise 3: China is now advancing technology rapidly. (Partially true)

This conclusion does not logically follow from the premises.
This is the key flaw.

2: The Critical Historical Distinction That Is Omitted
The invention of tools alone did not create the modern technological world.
The decisive factor was the emergence of a self-sustaining system of knowledge generation.
This system included:
The scientific method
Systematic experimentation
Mathematical modeling of nature
Institutionalized science
Open critique and falsification
Property rights and capital investment
Distributed innovation across independent actors
These emerged primarily in Europe between roughly 1500–1800.
This system produced continuous exponential technological advancement.
Before this system existed, inventions appeared sporadically across many civilizations but did not produce sustained technological acceleration.
China had paper and gunpowder centuries earlier but did not produce:
Industrialization
Modern physics
Electrical engineering
Computing
Aviation
The tools existed. The system did not.
The system is what matters most.

3: The Core Category Error in the Framing
Two different types of technological contribution are being conflated:
Type A: Foundational Paradigm Creation
Examples:
Scientific method
Newtonian physics
Electromagnetism
Semiconductor physics
Computing architectures
These change the trajectory of civilization itself.
Type B: Applied Engineering, Scaling, and Optimization
Examples:
Manufacturing efficiency improvements
Infrastructure deployment
Supply chain optimization
Incremental engineering improvements
These operate within an existing paradigm.
They are important but do not redefine the technological foundation.
Treating modern applied engineering leadership as equivalent to paradigm-defining inventions is not justified.

4: The Most Important Historical Fact
If paper, printing, compass, and gunpowder alone were sufficient to create the modern technological world, then industrialization would have occurred where those tools first existed.
It did not.
Industrialization occurred where the scientific method and institutionalized innovation emerged.
This demonstrates that tools alone are insufficient. The epistemological system is the decisive variable.

5: The Modern Claim Requires Precision
China is at the forefront in certain domains:
Manufacturing scale
Battery production
Infrastructure deployment
Telecommunications deployment
But these exist within the global technological framework already established.
This represents high-level participation within an existing system.
This is structurally different from originating the system itself.

6: The Precise Logical Counterpoint
The foundational transition to the modern technological world was not caused by the mere existence of enabling tools like paper or gunpowder. Those tools existed in multiple civilizations long before modern industrialization.
The decisive development was the emergence of the scientific method and institutionalized knowledge generation, which created a self-sustaining system of continuous discovery and technological advancement.
Early inventions were important enabling tools, but they did not produce modern technological civilization by themselves.
Modern strength in manufacturing and applied engineering reflects high capability within an existing technological paradigm, but this is categorically different from originating the foundational scientific framework that created the modern technological world.
This position is historically accurate and logically consistent.

7: The Core Insight
The modern technological world was not created by isolated inventions.
It was created by a system that continuously produces new inventions.
That system was the true breakthrough.
Tools accelerate progress. Systems sustain progress.
This distinction is the key to understanding the historical progression accurately.


What the Modern Era Actually Represents
The Modern Era is not defined primarily by the volume of technological production or manufacturing output.
Manufacturing scale, patent counts, and economic output measure execution capability within a system. They are quantitative indicators of activity, but they do not define the civilizational breakthrough itself.
The defining characteristic of the Modern Era was the emergence of a framework that enabled continuous human advancement. This included scientific rationalism, institutionalized inquiry, individual intellectual freedom, property rights, capital formation, and incentive structures that rewarded innovation and discovery.
This system produced modern medicine, dramatically increased human lifespan, industrial productivity, global communication, computing, and scientific advancement at an unprecedented scale.
These developments increased human flourishing, expanded individual capability, and created sustained technological progress across generations.
Economic and manufacturing output are measurable outcomes of this system, but they represent only one dimension of civilizational contribution.
The creation of a self-sustaining system of knowledge generation, innovation, and human advancement was the defining civilizational breakthrough of the Modern Era.

@saiansupereroe Western democracy increasingly functions as an illusion. Elections exist less to grant genuine political freedom than to persuade citizens that such freedom exists, while real political power remains concentrated in the hands of wealthy elites who wield disproportionate influence over media and public discourse. Two-party systems reinforce this illusion of choice: voters are offered competing labels rather than meaningful alternatives. In practice, neither side consistently produces leaders genuinely committed to the interests of ordinary citizens. Once elected, many officials primarily serve the oligarchs and corporate interests that financed their campaigns, not the public they claim to represent.

Similarly, the Philippines, despite decades of democratic elections, has failed to achieve sustained national progress and remains trapped in cycles of poverty, inequality, and political dynasties. These cases suggest that democratic form alone does not guarantee good governance, accountability, or development.

@MrGriff305-d3u If you’re going to dismiss paper and gunpowder as trivial, you’re arguing against basic world history.

Paper enabled mass literacy and bureaucracy which modern science is build on from knowledge transfer through generations. Printing enabled knowledge scaling. Gunpowder ended the era of armored aristocracies and reshaped global power structures. The compass enabled global navigation. Those aren’t “updates to papyrus.” They’re civilizational multipliers.

As for gunpowder and military relevance: China absolutely used it extensively (rockets, bombs, cannons) centuries before Europe refined it into modern artillery. But military dominance isn’t determined by one invention; it’s determined by geography, political structure, economic systems, and timing. The Ottoman Empire, Britain, and others leveraged gunpowder into global empires - that doesn’t erase where it originated. 

And since you brought up global reach: In the early 15th century, the admiral Zheng led massive treasure fleets across Southeast Asia, India, the Arabian Peninsula, and East Africa (1405-1433). These voyages involved ships far larger than those used by European explorers decades later. Yet China did not establish overseas colonies or engage in territorial conquest in Africa. The missions were primarily diplomatic and trade-oriented. China chose peace despite its technological capacity.

Now to the modern point. You’re framing innovation as if it only counts when it’s American, and manufacturing as if it’s somehow inferior. That’s outdated. 
-Over 70–80% of global solar panels are produced in China.
- The majority of EV batteries globally are produced by Chinese firms.
- China installs more industrial robots annually than the U.S. and Europe combined.
- It leads the world in patent filings and produces more STEM graduates each year than any other country.

That isn’t “cheap copying.” That’s scale, supply-chain control and industrial execution, which, in advanced manufacturing, is technological power.. Can the US do that? The answer is no, not because the US does not have cheap labor but because the US has no technology know-how of skilled labors.

And regarding the moon: the United States hasn’t repeated a crewed lunar landing since the Apollo era, Why is that? Because it no longer sees that as valuable. Why should China do something that does not add any value? Technological leadership today isn’t proven by reenacting 1969. It’s proven by frontier development in AI, semiconductor ecosystems, energy storage, telecom infrastructure, biotech, robotics, and advanced manufacturing.

No major power today invests billions in a mission purely for symbolism. They invest where it compounds economic and strategic capability.

Leadership now is about who controls production capacity, research volume, and deployment at scale, not who won a Cold War milestone half a century ago.

The reality is simple: the U.S. remains a technological superpower. China is also a technological superpower. The era of single-country monopoly is over.

If that feels uncomfortable, that’s not a historical argument, that’s nostalgia.

​@lamania32 Thank you for taking the time to explain your critique. I mean that sincerely. You’re pointing to a real limitation of AI, and it’s an important one to understand clearly.

My epistemic foundation didn’t come from AI. It developed from working through first principles—starting with the basic fact of experience itself. Experience implies interaction with something not fully under my voluntary control, which strongly suggests the existence of an external reality independent of belief. From there, logical consistency, empirical observation, and causal coherence emerge as the only reliable tools for navigating that reality.

That line of reasoning leads directly into the classical realist tradition, the scientific method, and Enlightenment rationalism—the idea that reality is structured, that reason can investigate it, and that knowledge can accumulate through disciplined inquiry.

Popper’s philosophy was especially important because it resolved the problem of certainty. He showed that knowledge does not advance by proving theories true, but by systematically eliminating false ones. This makes knowledge inherently provisional, but still capable of improving over time. Fallibilism becomes a strength, not a weakness, because it builds error correction directly into the system.

I also took postmodern and radical skeptical critiques seriously, because they raise legitimate challenges about certainty, bias, and the social context of knowledge. But when you follow radical skepticism to its logical end, it can’t escape relying on reason, coherence, and shared reality to make its own arguments. It ultimately reinforces the need for structured methods of inquiry rather than undermining them. In that sense, it strengthens the Enlightenment project by forcing it to become more self-critical and less dogmatic. (And as an aside, I'd argue this is the major split in the West right now - not a political split insomuch as an epistemic split - Modern vs Postmodern).

Your critique fits directly into that same fallibilist tradition. Steelmanning your point: AI generates persuasive structure without having independent access to truth. That creates a real risk that coherent presentation can increase confidence without increasing reliability. If someone begins relying on AI’s synthesis without maintaining independent verification, epistemic drift can occur without being noticed.

That’s a valid warning, and I take it seriously.

This is exactly where fallibilism becomes operational rather than abstract. Fallibilism means treating every tool, method, and conclusion—including AI-assisted reasoning and my own thinking—as potentially flawed and subject to correction. Your critique becomes part of the error-correction process itself.

The framework isn’t weakened by that critique—it’s strengthened by incorporating it as an additional safeguard. Epistemic authority remains grounded in evidence, logical consistency, and independent verification, not in any tool used to assist reasoning.

AI is useful because it accelerates structure and analysis. But fallibilism ensures that speed never replaces verification, and structure never replaces truth.

That constraint is the foundation of the entire process.

Here is the tricky part. You have no way of truly knowing if this is AI generated, I wrote it unaided, copied it from a book or spent years developing my own epistemology and ideas. You'll have to judge for yourself.

Gunpowder was first developed in China, not India. It was discovered by Chinese alchemists during the Tang Dynasty (9th century CE) while experimenting with sulfur, charcoal, and saltpeter. The earliest known written formula appears in the Chinese military text Wujing Zongyao (1044 CE).

From China, gunpowder technology spread westward via the Silk Road to the Islamic world, Indian subcontinent and later to Europe. The Phoenicians (c. 1500-300 BCE) were skilled navigators, but they navigated using:
- The sun
- The stars (especially Polaris)
- Coastal landmarks

@didierduplantier8359 Buddhism spreading from India to China has absolutely nothing to do with the origin of gunpowder. Religious transmission and technological invention are completely different historical processes. The fact that Buddhism traveled to China does not magically allow claims that every later Chinese inventions as Indian's.

As for the Shukraniti, any serious historians do not accept it as evidence that India invented gunpowder. The text’s dating is highly disputed, and the passages often cited are from much later manuscripts, many likely medieval or even early modern interpolations. There is no verified pre-9th-century Indian source that clearly describes the stable saltpeter-sulfur-charcoal formula used as true gunpowder.

By contrast, China has documented, datable, primary sources from the Tang period and the 1044 CE Wujing Zongyao that explicitly describe the formula and its military applications.

Surmising that China “must have lifted it” because Buddhism spread earlier is unfounded speculation, not evidence. Historical claims require contemporary documentation, not some made up national pride or retroactive interpretation.
